title: Less Language, More Latents: Annotation-Efficient VLAs for Driving
claim: Standard training needs dense, expensive multi-type language supervision on every frame; ours reaches comparable results with only a small fraction of labels.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right flow, red vs green dashed label boxes
description: Two side-by-side panels compare training setups. Panel (a), 'Standard VLA training', shows a driving camera observation on top. A red dashed box below holds four stacked label types: HLC, CF, VQA & HLC, and CoT & HLC. Each has dotted text boxes with example instructions or questions. Arrows lead into a large gray dashed block labelled 'VLA'. From it, arrows lead to trajectory icons, some paired with answer text boxes. A red banner at the bottom reads 'Driving datasets require labelling'. Panel (b), 'LADA (ours)', has the same observation image. A green dashed box holds only '~5% of HLC' and '~5% of CF'. These feed a gray 'LADA' block that outputs two trajectory icons. A green box states 'LADA learns using only ~5% of labels'. Red versus green coding and the much smaller input stack draw the eye first.
caption: LADA learns language-conditioned driving using $\sim$5% of language labels. (a) Standard VLA training requires every frame to be paired with rich linguistic supervision -- high-level commands (HLC), counterfactual instructions (CF), and auxiliary chain-of-thought (CoT) and VQA annotations -- all of which are expensive to acquire at scale. (b) LADA (ours) sidesteps this annotation bottleneck by exploiting the abundant observation-trajectory stream: trained with images alongside only $\sim$5% HLC and $\sim$5% CF annotations, with no CoT or VQA supervision, while still matching or exceeding fully-supervised baselines on closed-loop Bench2Drive.
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLA) promise human-steerable autonomous driving, but their training is bottlenecked by the scarcity of frames paired with natural-language instructions: while camera streams and expert trajectories are logged at scale, language annotations (e.g., turn left at the intersection) remain scarce and expensive to acquire. To address this challenge, we introduce Latent Action Driving Annotations (LADA), a three-stage pipeline that transforms abundant unlabelled observation-trajectory pairs into a substrate for language-conditioned control. First, we train a latent action model with a vector-quantised bottleneck, producing a compact codebook of high-level vehicle intents. Second, a small language-annotated subset is used to train a vision-language translator to map observations and language instructions into this codebook. Third, we train a driving VLA on observation-latent-action pairs over the full unlabelled corpus. Using fewer than 5% of language annotations and without leveraging any auxiliary chain-of-thought reasoning or visual question answering streams, LADA achieves a Driving Score of 87.98 and a Success Rate of 70.46% on the closed-loop Bench2Drive benchmark, matching or surpassing fully supervised baselines.
